segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: OK, Jim. You wanted to see me about your textile design project.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: That’s right. I’ve been looking at how a range of natural dyes can be used to colour fabrics like cotton and wool.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: Why did you choose that topic?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Well, I got a lot of useful ideas from the museum, you know, at that exhibition of textiles. But I’ve always been interested in anything to do with colour. Years ago, I went to a carpet shop with my parents when we were on holiday in Turkey, and I remember all the amazing colours.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: They might not all have been natural dyes.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Maybe not, but for the project I decided to follow it up. And I found a great book about a botanic garden in California that specialises in plants used for dyes.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: OK. So, in your project, you had to include a practical investigation.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Yeah. At first I couldn’t decide on my variables. I was going to just look at one type of fibre for example, like cotton ...

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: ... and see how different types of dyes affected it?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Yes. Then I decided to include others as well, so I looked at cotton and wool and nylon.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: With just one type of dye?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Various types, including some that weren’t natural, for comparison.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: OK.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: So, I did the experiments last week. I used some ready-made natural dyes. I found a website which supplied them, they came in just a few days, but I also made some of my own.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: That must have taken quite a bit of time.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Yes, I’d thought it’d just be a matter of a teaspoon or so of dye, and actually that wasn’t the case at all. Like I was using one vegetable, beetroot, for a red dye, and I had to chop up a whole pile of it. So it all took longer than I’d expected.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: One possibility is to use food colourings.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: I did use one. That was a yellow dye, an artificial one.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: Tartrazine?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Yeah. I used it on cotton first. It came out a great colour, but when I rinsed the material, the colour just washed away. I’d been going to try it out on nylon, but I abandoned that idea.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: Were you worried about health issues?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: I’d thought if it’s a legal food colouring, it must be safe.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: Well, it can occasionally cause allergic reactions, I believe. ———————–

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: So what natural dyes did you look at?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Well, one was turmeric. The colour’s great, it’s a really strong yellow. It’s generally used in dishes like curry.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: It’s meant to be quite good for your health when eaten, but you might find it’s not permanent when it’s used as a dye – a few washes, and it’s gone.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Right. I used beetroot as a dye for wool. When I chop up beetroot to eat I always end up with bright red hands, but the wool ended up just a sort of watery cream shade. Disappointing.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: There’s a natural dye called Tyrian purple. Have you heard of that?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Yes. It comes from a shellfish, and it was worn in ancient times but only by important people as it was so rare. I didn’t use it.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: It fell out of use centuries ago, though one researcher managed to get hold of some recently. But that shade of purple can be produced by chemical dyes nowadays. Did you use any black dyes?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Logwood. That was quite complicated. I had to prepare the fabric so the dye would take.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: I hope you were careful to wear gloves.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Yes. I know the danger with that dye.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: Good. It can be extremely dangerous if it’s ingested. Now, presumably you had a look at an insect-based dye? Like cochineal, for example?

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: Yes. I didn’t actually make that, I didn’t have time to start crushing up insects to get the red colour and anyway they’re not available here, but I managed to get the dye quite easily from a website. But it cost a fortune. I can see why it’s generally just used in cooking, and in small quantities.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: Yes, it’s very effective, but that’s precisely why it’s not used as a dye.

segments.speaker: JIM
segments.en: I also read about using metal oxide. Apparently you can allow iron to rust while it’s in contact with the fabric, and that colours it.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.en: Yes, that works well for dying cotton. But you have to be careful as the metal can actually affect the fabric and so you can’t expect to get a lot of wear out of fabrics treated in this way. And the colours are quite subtle, not everyone likes them. Anyway, it looks as if you’ve done a lot of work...

SECTION 3
Questions 21-30
PROJECT ON USING NATURAL DYES TO COLOUR FABRICS
Choose the correct letter A, B or C.
Questions:
    Q Num: 21
    Text: What first inspired Jim to choose this project?
    Options:
        textiles displayed in an exhibition.
        a book about a botanic garden.
        carpets he saw on holiday.
    Q Num: 22
    Text: Jim eventually decided to do a practical investigation which involved
    Options:
        using a range of dyes with different fibres.
        applying different dyes to one type of fibre.
        testing one dye and a range of fibres.
    Q Num: 23
    Text: When doing his experiments, Jim was surprised by
    Options:
        how much natural material was needed to make the dye.
        the fact that dyes were widely available on the internet.
        the time that he had to leave the fabric in the dye.
    Q Num: 24
    Text: What problem did Jim have with using tartrazine as a fabric dye?
    Options:
        It caused a slight allergic reaction.
        It was not a permanent dye on cotton.
        It was ineffective when used on nylon.
Problems
What problem is identified with each of the following natural dyes?
Choose SIX answers from the box and write the correct letter A–H next to questions 25–30.
